newsitem.title: UK: Major warns of divorce between Scotland, England.
newsitem.headline: Major warns of divorce between Scotland, England.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major highlighted on Thursday his fear of a divorce between Scotland and England if he loses the May 1 election by visiting a Scottish border village famous for runaway marriages.

After touring a blacksmith's shop in Gretna Green, a village on the Scottish border that became popular last century as Britain's elopement capital for English couples seeking a quick wedding, Major said: "I am here to give my pledge to the union between Scotland and Wales, Northern Ireland and England."
Major, whose party lags its Labour opponents by some 20 points in the polls, hopes to win back key voters by emphasising concerns that a Labour government would lead to a break-up of Britain.
Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats have pledged to set up separate Scottish and Welsh parliaments to give people in the two countries greater control over their own affairs.
Major said this would be the first step on a slippery slope to a fully independent Scotland.
"In just four weeks' time Britain will make a momentous decision," he said.

"We will have to decide whether we want a prosperous United Kingdom speaking as one nation in the forums of the world, or as a divided country washed up on the wider shores of separatism with the inevitable bitterness that would follow."
Conservative campaign organisers chose Gretna Green as the venue for Major's first election campaign foray north of the border partly because it is in the relatively marginal seat of Dumfries.
With support for the Conservatives in Scotland at a dismal 12 percent according to one recent poll, prospective candidate Struan Stevenson needs help in defending a 6,415-vote Conservative majority.
An aide to Major said the village was also a symbol of the sanctity of marriage, both between couples and between Scotland and England.

From 1753 to 1940, thousands of English couples refused permission by their parents to marry eloped to Gretna Green where Scots law, separate from that in England, allowed them to wed with little delay.

It was the 19th century's answer to Las Vegas, requiring only that couples declare their wish to marry before witnesses. They took their vows over an anvil in the village blacksmith's shop until a World War Two act of parliament outlawed "anvil marriages".
